examples.knowledge_point: Solving Exponential Equations Containing Different Bases by Rewriting Two Exponents
examples.worked_solution:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base. To do this, we rewrite the equation using $9={\color{red}3}^2$ and $27 = {\color{red}3}^3,$ as follows:

$$
\left({\color{red}3}^2\right)^{3x}=\left({\color{red}3}^3\right)^{x+2}
$$

Then, we apply the power rule for exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2(3x)}={3}^{3(x+2)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since both sides of the equation share the same base $({\color{red}3}),$ we equate the exponents and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(3x) & =3(x+2) \\ 6x & =3x+6 \\ 3x & =6 \\ x & =2\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
To solve this equation, we need both exponential terms to have a common base.

To do this, we write $25$ as ${5}^{2},$ and then we rewrite the right-hand side using the power rule of exponents:

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2a-5} & =\frac{1}{{25}^{a+1}} \\ {5}^{2a-5} & =\frac{1}{{({5}^{2})}^{a+1}} \\ {5}^{2a-5} & =\frac{1}{{5}^{2(a+1)}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using a negative exponent: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{5}^{2a-5} & ={5}^{-2(a+1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since both sides of the equation share the same base $(5)$, we equate the exponents and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2a-5 & =-2(a+1) \\ 2a-5 & =-2a-2 \\ 4a & =3 \\ a & =\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$
